## Two Proportions {#sec-two-proportions}

```{r}
#| label: setup-3-1
#| include: false
source(if (file.exists("R/setup.R")) "R/setup.R" else "../R/setup.R")

# All quantities for comparing two proportions, rounded as in the book
two_prop <- function(x1, n1, x2, n2) {
  p1 <- x1 / n1; p2 <- x2 / n2
  se <- round(sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n1 + p2 * (1 - p2) / n2), 4)
  pbar <- round((x1 + x2) / (n1 + n2), 4)
  se0 <- round(sqrt(pbar * (1 - pbar) * (1 / n1 + 1 / n2)), 4)
  list(x1 = x1, n1 = n1, x2 = x2, n2 = n2, p1 = p1, p2 = p2, d = p1 - p2,
       se = se, pbar = pbar, se0 = se0, z = round((p1 - p2) / se0, 3))
}
```

### Learning Objectives

1. Construct and interpret a confidence interval for the difference $p_1 - p_2$.
2. Carry out a $z$ test for $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ using the pooled proportion.
3. Explain why the test pools the two samples but the CI does not.

### Concept

We often compare two groups: urban and rural households, men and women in the
labour force, customers of two brands. The parameter of interest is the
difference $p_1 - p_2$, estimated by $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$. For two
independent random samples that are large enough, $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is
approximately normal with standard error
$$
\sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}.
$$

The same idea as in Section 2.3 decides which values go into the standard error:

- **Confidence interval:** use $\hat{p}_1$ and $\hat{p}_2$ separately.
- **Hypothesis test:** $H_0$ says $p_1 = p_2$, so both groups share one
  proportion. Our best estimate of it combines the two samples, the
  **pooled proportion**
$$
\bar{p} = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{n_1 + n_2}.
$$

### Formulas and Conditions

**Conditions:** two independent random samples; $n\hat{p} \ge 5$ and
$n(1-\hat{p}) \ge 5$ in each sample.

**$(1-\alpha)100\%$ confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$**
$$
(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}
$$

**Test statistic** for $H_0: p_1 = p_2$
$$
z_{\text{cal}} = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2}
{\sqrt{\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}\right)}}
$$

| $H_1$ | Critical region |
|:---:|:---|
| $p_1 \ne p_2$ | $z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha/2}$ or $z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}$ |
| $p_1 < p_2$ | $z_{\text{cal}} < z_{\alpha}$ |
| $p_1 > p_2$ | $z_{\text{cal}} > z_{1-\alpha}$ |

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-1
a <- two_prop(171, 300, 165, 250)
a_me <- crit_z(.975) * a$se
```

### Example

**Example 3.1.1.** A survey asks households whether they have any
outstanding debt. In urban areas, `r a$x1` of `r a$n1` households have debt; in
rural areas, `r a$x2` of `r a$n2` households have debt.

(a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the difference between the urban and rural proportions.
(b) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the proportion of households with debt is different in urban and rural areas.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=false}
## Solution

Let group 1 = urban and group 2 = rural.
$\hat{p}_1 = `r a$x1`/`r a$n1` = `r num(a$p1)`$, $\hat{p}_2 = `r a$x2`/`r a$n2` = `r num(a$p2)`$,
$\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = `r num(a$d)`$.

**(a)**
$$
\sqrt{\frac{`r num(a$p1)`(`r num(1 - a$p1)`)}{`r a$n1`} + \frac{`r num(a$p2)`(`r num(1 - a$p2)`)}{`r a$n2`}} = `r num(a$se)`
$$
$$
`r num(a$d)` \pm `r fmt(crit_z(.975), 3)`(`r num(a$se)`) = `r num(a$d)` \pm `r num(a_me)`
$$
95% CI: (`r fmt(a$d - a_me, 4)`, `r fmt(a$d + a_me, 4)`)

We are 95% confident that the difference between the urban and rural
proportions of households with debt is between `r fmt(a$d - a_me, 4)` and
`r fmt(a$d + a_me, 4)`. Both limits are negative, so the urban proportion is
lower.

**(b)**

**Step 1: Hypotheses.** $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ $\quad H_1: p_1 \ne p_2$

**Step 2: Level of significance.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3: Test statistic.**
$$
\bar{p} = \frac{`r a$x1` + `r a$x2`}{`r a$n1` + `r a$n2`} = `r num(a$pbar)`
$$
$$
z_{\text{cal}} = \frac{`r num(a$d)`}
{\sqrt{`r num(a$pbar)`(`r num(1 - a$pbar)`)\left(\frac{1}{`r a$n1`} + \frac{1}{`r a$n2`}\right)}}
= \frac{`r num(a$d)`}{`r num(a$se0)`} = `r fmt(a$z, 3)`
$$

**Step 4: Critical value and critical region.**
Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-crit_z(.975), 3)`$ or $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(crit_z(.975), 3)`$.

**Step 5: Decision and interpretation.**
$z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(a$z, 3)`$ falls in the critical region
($`r fmt(a$z, 3)` < `r fmt(-crit_z(.975), 3)`$), so we reject $H_0$.
That is, the proportion of households with debt is different in urban and rural
areas at the 0.05 level of significance; since $\hat{p}_1 < \hat{p}_2$, the
proportion is lower in urban areas.
:::

```{r}
#| label: yt-3-1
b <- two_prop(58, 200, 36, 180)
b_me <- crit_z(.975) * b$se
```

### Your Turn

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Your Turn 3.1.1

Two brands of instant noodles raised their prices by the same amount. Of
`r b$n1` regular customers of Brand A, `r b$x1` switched to another brand; of
`r b$n2` regular customers of Brand B, `r b$x2` switched.

(a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for $p_A - p_B$.
(b) At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether the proportion of customers who switched is higher for Brand A.
:::

::: {.workspace lines="4"}
:::

::: {.workspace steps="names"}
:::

::: {.answer title="Your Turn 3.1.1"}
$\hat{p}_A = `r num(b$p1)`$, $\hat{p}_B = `r num(b$p2)`$, $\hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B = `r num(b$d)`$.

**(a)** SE $= `r num(b$se)`$;
$`r num(b$d)` \pm `r fmt(crit_z(.975), 3)`(`r num(b$se)`) = `r num(b$d)` \pm `r num(b_me)`$.
95% CI: (`r fmt(b$d - b_me, 4)`, `r fmt(b$d + b_me, 4)`). We are 95% confident that
the difference between the proportions of Brand A and Brand B customers who
switched is between `r fmt(b$d - b_me, 4)` and `r fmt(b$d + b_me, 4)`.

**(b)**

**Step 1.** $H_0: p_A = p_B \quad H_1: p_A > p_B$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $\bar{p} = (`r b$x1` + `r b$x2`)/(`r b$n1` + `r b$n2`) = `r num(b$pbar)`$;
$z_{\text{cal}} = `r num(b$d)`/`r num(b$se0)` = `r fmt(b$z, 3)`$

**Step 4.** $z_{0.95} = `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$. Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} > `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$.

**Step 5.** $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(b$z, 3)`$ falls in the critical region
($`r fmt(b$z, 3)` > `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$), so we reject $H_0$.
That is, the proportion of customers who switched is higher for Brand A than for
Brand B at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::

### Looking Back: Methods So Far

| Parameter | Estimate | Distribution | Section |
|:---|:---|:---|:---:|
| $\mu$ ($\sigma$ known) | $\bar{x}$ | $z$ | 2.1 |
| $\mu$ ($\sigma$ unknown) | $\bar{x}$ | $t$, df $= n-1$ | 2.2 |
| $p$ | $\hat{p}$ | $z$ | 2.3 |
| $\sigma^2$ | $s^2$ | $\chi^2$, df $= n-1$ | 2.4 |
| $p_1 - p_2$ | $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ | $z$ | 3.1 |

Every test so far followed the same five steps and made the decision with the
critical region. Section 3.2 introduces a second way to make the decision, the
p-value, and shows how to read the results from R.

### Formula Summary

| | Confidence interval | Hypothesis test |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Standard error | $\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}$ | $\sqrt{\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1}+\dfrac{1}{n_2}\right)}$, $\bar{p} = \dfrac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}$ |
| Formula | $(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2) \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\text{SE}$ | $z_{\text{cal}} = \dfrac{\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2}{\text{SE}}$ |

```{r}
#| label: ex-3-1-exercises
e1 <- two_prop(45, 150, 62, 160); e1_me <- crit_z(.95) * e1$se
e2 <- two_prop(84, 240, 96, 240)
```

### Exercises

**3.1.1** In a labour force survey, `r e1$x1` of `r e1$n1` women and `r e1$x2`
of `r e1$n2` men aged 15--24 were not in employment, education or training. Construct a 90% confidence interval for
$p_{\text{women}} - p_{\text{men}}$.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.1.1"}
$\hat{p}_1 = `r num(e1$p1)`$, $\hat{p}_2 = `r num(e1$p2)`$, difference $= `r num(e1$d)`$,
SE $= `r num(e1$se)`$, $z_{0.95} = `r fmt(crit_z(.95), 3)`$.
$`r num(e1$d)` \pm `r num(e1_me)`$: 90% CI (`r fmt(e1$d - e1_me, 4)`, `r fmt(e1$d + e1_me, 4)`).
We are 90% confident that the difference between the proportions of women and men
not in employment, education or training is between `r fmt(e1$d - e1_me, 4)` and
`r fmt(e1$d + e1_me, 4)`. The interval contains 0.
:::

**3.1.2** A shop tests two price displays. With display 1, `r e2$x1` of
`r e2$n1` visitors bought the product; with display 2, `r e2$x2` of `r e2$n2`
bought it. At $\alpha$ = 0.05, test whether display 1
has a lower purchase rate.

::: {.answer title="Exercise 3.1.2"}
**Step 1.** $H_0: p_1 = p_2 \quad H_1: p_1 < p_2$

**Step 2.** $\alpha$ = 0.05

**Step 3.** $\hat{p}_1 = `r num(e2$p1)`$, $\hat{p}_2 = `r num(e2$p2)`$, $\bar{p} = `r num(e2$pbar)`$;
$z_{\text{cal}} = `r num(e2$d)`/`r num(e2$se0)` = `r fmt(e2$z, 3)`$

**Step 4.** $z_{0.05} = `r fmt(-crit_z(.95), 3)`$. Critical region: $z_{\text{cal}} < `r fmt(-crit_z(.95), 3)`$.

**Step 5.** $z_{\text{cal}} = `r fmt(e2$z, 3)`$ does not fall in the critical region
($`r fmt(e2$z, 3)` > `r fmt(-crit_z(.95), 3)`$), so we accept $H_0$.
That is, the purchase rates with the two displays are equal at the 0.05 level of significance.
:::
